newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters cement role of Freedom to Farm law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters cement role of Freedom to Farm law.

text.p: The landmark "Freedom to Farm" law, which ended most federal control over farmers, is now safe from attack in Congress, leading lawmakers said Wednesday, despite electoral attacks by populist Democrats.

President Clinton reluctantly signed "Freedom to Farm" into law in April and repeatedly said he would try to strengthen its safety net next year. But any administration proposals will be aimed at fine-tuning the law, rather than rewriting it, said an aide to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.

Leaders of the House and Senate Agriculture committees said their agendas for 1997 would focus on trade issues and a review of agricultural research programs that spend $1 billion a year. Forestry, alternative fuels, rural development and a tightening of commodity-trading laws also were on the list.
Oregon Republican Bob Smith, tabbed to chair the House Agriculture Committee, said he wanted to "revisit NAFTA" because of complaints of unfairly priced Mexican cattle and Canadian barley and wheat.
"Somebody has to stand up for those commodities," Smith said in an interview. "This administration won't do it."

Three members of the House Agriculture Committee were elected to the Senate. Winners were chairman Pat Roberts, Kansas Republican, Colorado Republican Wayne Allard and Democrat Tim Johnson of South Dakota.
By retaining control of Congress, Republicans blunted chances to revise their brainchild, "Freedom to Farm."

The most sweeping change in U.S. farm policy in 60 years, "Freedom to Farm" allows farmers to plant nearly any crop they want but puts an annual limit on farm subsidy payments, $5.4 billion this fiscal year and dropping to $4 billion in fiscal 2002 -- half the annual cost of the 1990 farm law.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said before Tuesday's elections that he hoped to replace "Freedom to Farm" with another subsidy plan, such as "marketing loans." "I think we're going to have to play out the hand
we were dealt on that one ('Freedom to Farm')," said Texan Charles Stenholm, likely to be the Democratic leader on the House Agriculture Committee.
Stenholm said Democrats would have a larger voice in farm legislation in the new Congress because Republicans would be less ideological than during the past two years.
"I can guarantee...we won't be kowtowing to our leadership like it was in the past two years," Stenholm said.
